intro: The second movement of Mahler’s Symphony No. 5, marked Stürmisch bewegt, mit größter Vehemenz, follows the opening funeral march. It is in A minor and includes a lament for the cellos. Near the end the brass play a chorale in D major, which then breaks off.

sections.label: A · Running basses and full-orchestra chords
sections.mNote: Low strings play a five-note figure against full-orchestra chords.

sections.label: B · Funeral-march theme in the cellos
sections.mNote: Four flats, at the first movement’s tempo

sections.label: A′ · Return of the running string figures
sections.mNote: The opening figures return and interrupt the cello theme.

sections.label: B′ · Cellos over a timpani roll
sections.mNote: A long E♭-minor melody with scarcely any accompaniment

sections.label: Dev · March theme and storm material
sections.mNote: A faster march in a major key, then the storm music returns.

sections.label: C · Brass chorale in D major
sections.mNote: Long brass chords above racing strings and harp

sections.label: Coda · storm figures return in scraps
sections.mNote: Short string figures continue as the brass chorale fades.

cues.title: Opening figure, cellos, basses and bassoons
cues.text: Cellos, basses and bassoons open at fff with a five-note figure that rises two steps and falls back. A rit. slows it before each hard orchestral chord. Mahler’s footnote says the pause gathers force and the figure itself stays fast; the marking is Mit grösster Vehemenz, with the greatest vehemence.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 48: Stürmisch bewegt. Mit grösster Vehemenz.; the figure in bassoons, cellos and basses marked fff with rit. and a tempo; the conductor’s footnote ends “Die Figur selbst muss im schnellen Tempo ausgeführt werden.” Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide describes the opening as motivic fragments, descending lines, harsh dissonances and a loud dynamic: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cello melody at rehearsal 5
cues.text: The rapid woodwind notes stop and a timpani roll remains. At rehearsal 5 Mahler writes Bedeutend langsamer (im Tempo des ersten Satzes “Trauermarsch”), much slower, in the tempo of the funeral march. The cellos then begin a lament in four flats, marked molto cantando.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 57–58, rehearsal 5: timpani roll mf to pp; Bedeutend langsamer (im Tempo des ersten Satzes „Trauermarsch“); cellos molto cantando, four flats. Basinger: the lyrical cello melody enters in the tempo of the first movement’s funeral march, molto cantando, in a minor key: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cello theme, clarinets and violins
cues.text: The cello theme is taken up by other instruments. Clarinets and bass clarinet add a counter-melody marked etwas hervortretend, slightly to the fore. The first violins then play the tune, marked zart, over pizzicato violas, cellos and basses.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 58: bass clarinet and clarinets etwas hervortretend, espress.; p. 60: first violins (zart) over pizzicato violas, cellos and basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition at Maiernigg, 1901–02
cues.text: Mahler began the Fifth in the summer of 1901. When he returned to Maiernigg the following summer he had met and married Alma Schindler, and they were expecting their first child. He composed the symphony over those two summers.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, Symphony No. 5 introduction: composition in 1901–02 and the family chronology. https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/

cues.title: Start of the development
cues.text: The opening figure returns ff in cellos, basses and bassoons, with horns stopped and trumpets muted. This begins the development, which brings back the motives of the movement’s opening.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 66: the figure in bassoons, contrabassoon, cellos and basses ff; horns gestopft, trumpets mit Dämpfer. Basinger: the development reintroduces the turbulent mood of the Stürmisch bewegt and its motives: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cellos over a timpani roll
cues.text: Marked pp klagend am Griffbrett (plaintive, bowed near the fingerboard), the cellos return to their melody in E♭ minor. A timpani roll continues beneath, and the violas hold a single sustained note; there is little other accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 70–71: rit., then six flats and Langsam aber immer; cellos pp klagend am Griffbrett, timpani roll throughout, violas am Griffbrett on a sustained note. Basinger: the cello melody returns marked klagend above an ominous timpani roll: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rehearsal 12, two horns
cues.text: At rehearsal 12 Mahler returns to Tempo moderato (wie im ersten Teil). Two horns, marked espress. and zart hervortretend, play the melody over rapid repeated notes in flutes, clarinets and bassoons.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 71, rehearsal 12: Tempo moderato (wie im ersten Teil); horns espress., zart hervortretend over repeated notes in the woodwinds. Basinger: the music after the klagend return varies the cello melody and combines it with material from the Trauermarsch: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Publication and revisions, 1904–1964
cues.text: Peters published the Fifth in 1904, and a second edition in 1905 carried Mahler’s revisions of 1904. His last corrections, made in 1911, were not printed until 1964.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s history page for the symphony gives the 1904 and 1905 Peters editions and the 1911 revisions printed in 1964: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-history/ . The Aspen Music Festival programme note says Mahler kept touching up the scoring almost until he died: https://www.aspenmusicfestival.com/program_notes/view/mahler-symphony-no.-5-in-c-sharp-minor

cues.title: Più mosso subito, march in major
cues.text: Mahler marked the change Più mosso subito, aber immer noch nicht so schnell wie zu Anfang: suddenly faster, though still slower than the opening tempo. The funeral music changes to a march in a major key, which gains in intensity as it goes.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 78, rehearsal 16: Più mosso subito, aber immer noch nicht so schnell wie zu Anfang. Basinger: the composer brusquely switches to a faster-moving march in a major key that gains in intensity: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Brass chorale and recapitulation
cues.text: The march broadens into a brass chorale over a ringing triangle, with timpani punctuating. The stormy motives of the opening break in, and the recapitulation begins.
cues.evidence: Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the march broadens into a brass chorale resounding over a ringing triangle with dramatic timpani punctuation; unable to sustain itself, it gives way as the stormy motives intrude and the recapitulation begins: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/

cues.title: Climax in D major, brass
cues.text: At the high point of the movement the brass hold long chords in D major, two sharps. Strings play rushing upward scales and the harp adds rising runs at fff, with cymbals struck mit Teller. The symphony ends in D major.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 102: two sharps; horns, trumpets and trombones on sustained chords; harp fff rising runs; Becken mit Teller; rushing scales in violins, violas, cellos and basses. Basinger: the movement reaches an extended peak in a D-major chorale, a key with significant implications for the rest of the symphony: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: End of the chorale; coda
cues.text: The chorale fades. Mahler marks Ritenuto, the brass chords die away to pp and the strings are marked morendo. The stormy opening motives return for the coda, and the chorale comes back at the high point of the finale.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 107: Ritenuto, diminuendo in the brass, harp arpeggios, strings morendo. Basinger: the Stürmisch bewegt motives resurface as the coda begins and prove short-lived (second movement); a chorale from this movement returns at the high point of the finale (fifth movement): https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars
cues.text: In the last pages, isolated wind and harp notes sound over soft string chords. The cellos and basses play a final ppp pizzicato figure and the timpani a last soft note. Mahler then wrote folgt lange Pause, a long pause follows.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 116–117: sparse wind, harp and triangle notes over divided strings; last bars poco rit., cellos and basses Tutti pizz. ppp, timpani p (gut stimmen!), “(folgt lange Pause.)”. Basinger: the anguished sigh remains until the composer silences it: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Timpani roll, then the cellos
transitions.from: A · Running basses and full-orchestra chords
transitions.to: B · Funeral-march theme in the cellos
transitions.how: The fast woodwind figures, marked Sehr drängend, break off over a timpani roll that falls from mf to pp. At rehearsal 5, marked Bedeutend langsamer, Mahler returns to the tempo of the first movement’s funeral march. The key signature changes to four flats, and the cellos play molto cantando.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 57–58: Sehr drängend, timpani roll mf to pp, rehearsal 5 Bedeutend langsamer (im Tempo des ersten Satzes „Trauermarsch“), cellos molto cantando.

transitions.title: The opening figure returns
transitions.from: B · Funeral-march theme in the cellos
transitions.to: A′ · Return of the running string figures
transitions.how: The song is cut off. The opening figure returns at ff in bassoons, contrabassoon, cellos and basses, with horns stopped and trumpets muted, and the development takes up the motives of the opening again.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 66: the opening figure in bassoons, contrabassoon, cellos and basses ff; horns gestopft, trumpets mit Dämpfer. Basinger: the development reintroduces the turbulent mood and its motives.

transitions.title: Timpani roll into the E♭-minor section
transitions.from: A′ · Return of the running string figures
transitions.to: B′ · Cellos over a timpani roll
transitions.how: The tempo slows at a rit. and a timpani roll takes over. The key signature changes to six flats with the marking Langsam aber immer. The cellos begin a slower melody in E♭ minor, pp klagend am Griffbrett, and the violas, also am Griffbrett, hold a long note beneath.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 70–71: rit., change to six flats, Langsam aber immer, cellos pp klagend am Griffbrett, timpani roll, violas am Griffbrett.

transitions.title: D major in brass above strings
transitions.from: Dev · March theme and storm material
transitions.to: C · Brass chorale in D major
transitions.how: The key signature changes to two sharps and D major arrives in sustained chords for horns, trumpets and trombones. The strings play rushing scales upward, the harp adds rising runs marked fff, and the cymbals are struck with a plate (“Becken mit Teller”).
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 102: two sharps, sustained chords in horns, trumpets and trombones, harp fff runs, Becken mit Teller, rushing string scales.

transitions.title: From the brass chorale to the coda
transitions.from: C · Brass chorale in D major
transitions.to: Coda · storm figures return in scraps
transitions.how: At Ritenuto the D-major brass chords make a diminuendo to pp, the harp plays a few arpeggios and the strings fade morendo. The motives of the Stürmisch bewegt opening return as the coda begins and are short-lived.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 107: Ritenuto, brass diminuendo to pp, harp arpeggios, strings morendo. Basinger: the Stürmisch bewegt motives resurface as the coda begins and prove short-lived.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, II, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed p. 48: rushing low strings and orchestral attacks; pp. 57–58: slow cello melody; p. 102: brass chorale; pp. 107–116: withdrawal and coda.

timeline.note: Running low strings and bassoons meet sharp orchestral attacks.
The woodwind figures soften above held notes in the lower instruments.
The cellos play the slower melody, with sparse woodwinds and bass punctuation.
The brass chorale opens above moving strings and harp.
Brass chords and low instruments fade after the chorale.
Quiet upper strings, scraps of woodwind melody and isolated harp notes finish the movement.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor, and that career would pay for everything else.
